summary: Describes a framework for Realm Specific IP (RSIP), an alternative to network address translation. With RSIP, a host borrows addressing parameters from a gateway so packets keep their end-to-end integrity. The document covers implementation issues, deployment scenarios, and interaction with other layer-three protocols. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Realm Specific IP (RSIP) is a framework for giving a host temporary use of address information from another network. The host tunnels its packets to an RSIP gateway, which forwards them without changing the inner packet's addresses.

questions: alternative to nat that preserves end-to-end
how does rsip differ from nat
subtitle: A framework for lending hosts network addresses instead of rewriting their packets.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translation changes packet headers, which can interfere with protocols that depend on end-to-end packet integrity.
tldr.mechanism: Realm Specific IP (RSIP) lets a host borrow addressing parameters from a gateway and tunnel packets through it, so the gateway can route replies back to that host.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Experimental framework and notes that complete RSIP deployments require changes to hosts and gateways and can create operational complications.

today: RFC 3102 is Experimental. Its IESG note calls out implementation changes and operational complications that should be weighed when considering RSIP.

sections.title: An Alternative to Address Translation
sections.content:
A Network Address Translation (NAT) router changes network-layer headers and may also change transport-layer headers. That can interfere with protocols that expect packet contents to remain intact from one endpoint to the other.

RSIP takes a different approach: a host borrows addresses or other routing parameters from a gateway in another addressing realm. The gateway forwards packets between the realms and keeps the information needed to direct incoming traffic back to the borrowing host.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of rewriting a packet, RSIP lets a host use address information supplied by a gateway. The host sends packets through a tunnel, and the gateway routes replies back.

sections.title: Hosts, Gateways, and Bindings
sections.content:
An RSIP host first obtains resources from an RSIP gateway. The gateway records a binding between the host's private addressing information and the borrowed public parameters, so it can identify the host when a reply arrives.

In RSA-IP, a host leases a public IP address. In RSAP-IP, hosts can share an address but lease distinct ports or other packet fields that let the gateway distinguish them. Hosts tunnel packets to the gateway, which removes the outer tunnel headers and forwards the inner packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway records which borrowed address or address-and-port values belong to each host. That record lets it send incoming packets through the tunnel to the correct host.

sections.title: What Hosts and Gateways Must Do
sections.content:
An RSIP host must support virtual interfaces for borrowed addresses and must be able to tunnel packets to an RSIP gateway. An RSIP gateway must terminate those tunnels, manage assigned resources, and reassemble incoming public-network fragments so it can route them to a host.

For shared addresses, the gateway relies on demultiplexing fields such as protocol, destination port, or other agreed packet fields. Encrypted fields cannot be used for that routing decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Both the host and gateway need tunneling support. The gateway also needs visible packet information that distinguishes each host when several hosts share an address.

sections.title: Deployment and Complications
sections.content:
The RFC discusses deployment scenarios, interaction with other network-layer protocols, and complications such as fragment handling, application servers, and multi-party applications. RSIP can be combined with NAT for hosts that do not support RSIP.

The IESG note warns that a complete implementation requires significant host and gateway changes, and that port assignment can prevent transparent operation for some applications. The RFC advises weighing RSIP's costs and benefits against other ways to address address shortages.
sections.plainLanguage: RSIP preserves packet contents in some cases, but it adds host, gateway, and operational requirements. The RFC warns that some applications may not work transparently with it.
